response:
Speculative decoding's acceptance rate is highly sensitive to the token distribution gap between draft and target models — but the collapse is non-linear and threshold-like rather than gradual. A striking demonstration comes from work analyzing SpecInfer and related systems: when the draft model is trained on a domain-shifted corpus (e.g., a code-specialized draft paired with a general-purpose target like LLaMA-2-70B), acceptance rates can crater from ~75% to under 30% even when perplexity on the target distribution degrades only modestly (e.g., 2–3 PPL points). The mechanism is that speculative decoding acceptance under the standard rejection-sampling correction (from Leviathan et al., 2023) is governed by the ratio min(1, p_target(x)/p_draft(x)) at each token position; a fat-tailed mismatch in even a small fraction of high-frequency tokens — punctuation, connectives, subword splits — can poison entire multi-token speculative windows because the window is accepted jointly, so one bad token collapses the whole span. This interacts badly with vocabulary mismatches in cross-tokenizer speculative setups (e.g., pairing a Medusa head trained on one tokenizer with a target using byte-level BPE), where there is no clean 1-to-1 token correspondence and researchers have found that naive token alignment strategies can reduce effective acceptance length from ~3.5 tokens per step to under 1.5. Distillation-based draft models (like those used in DeepMind's Graphcore speculative work and Meta's experiments with Eagle/Eagle-2) specifically target this by training the draft to minimize KL divergence at the distribution level against the target, rather than just minimizing cross-entropy on the target's output text — and this distinction meaningfully recovers acceptance rates in domain-shifted inference scenarios.
